comment: Every difference between stack-up, stack-single and stack-k8s that somebody
has looked at and decided to keep. C5 fails on any divergence NOT recorded
here, and also on any entry here that is no longer a divergence.
'agreed' per family is the value the three are measured against. It is not
a majority vote and not an average: it is what the estate says the stack
is. Changing an 'agreed' value is a decision about the product, not a way
Provenance markers follow the estate convention: @claude is a reading of
the code and should be re-checked, @yurii is a decision, @measured names
the run that established it. Everything in this file was written by
reading the three repositories on 2026-08-06 and is therefore @claude.
The reasons are the honest state of the estate on that date, which in
several cases is 'this is a gap, not a decision'. That is deliberate: a
gap recorded as a gap is still better than a gap nobody wrote down, and
the entry is what makes it visible enough to close.

routines.what: Governance routines each deployment installs, by canonical kind.

routines:stack-up:disabled:mockryx-drill.why: Deliberate and documented in stack-up/routines.sh: mockryx-drill is opt-in behind --with-drill and never in DEFAULT_ROUTINES, because a fire drill spends real gateway budget against a live box. The other four are safe to run unattended.

routines:stack-k8s:disabled:mockryx-dril.why: Same decision as stack-up, expressed as `suspend: true` on the `drills` CronJob. The operator unsuspends it when they want a drill.

routines:stack-k8s:absent:trailryx-seal.why: A GAP, not a decision, and the decision behind that word is his: asked directly whether all three deployments are meant to seal the record, he said all three are. stack-up runs trailryx-node events over the shared event directory and gets an offline-verifiable record of what the stack did; a Kubernetes install gets none. Measured 2026-08-25: stack-k8s does not mention trailryx anywhere at all, not in a manifest and not in a comment, so this is not a routine that was considered and left out. Recorded here so the day somebody closes it, this entry goes red as stale and gets removed.

routines:stack-single:absent:trailryx-se.why: The same gap, on the deployment that already installs no governance routine of any kind. Measured 2026-08-25: stack-single does not mention trailryx anywhere. It is the single-box install, which is the one most likely to be somebody's first look at the estate, and it produces no sealed record of anything it did.

routines:stack-k8s:absent:focus-export.why: A GAP, not a decision. Four of the five governance routines have a CronJob and focus-export does not, so a Kubernetes install produces no focus export at all. stack-k8s's own manifest comment calls it a finding rather than an oversight, which records it without closing it. Recorded here so the day somebody closes it, this entry goes red as stale and gets removed.

routines:stack-single:absent:focus-expor.why: stack-single installs NO governance routine of any kind: no cron, no timer, no supervisor, no periodic compose service. Searched across compose.yaml, install.sh and the whole repo on 2026-08-06. It is the single-box deployment and it brings up the planes without the scheduled work that keeps them producing. This is the largest unrecorded difference of the three and it is a gap, not a decision.

routines:stack-single:absent:mockryx-dri.why: See routines:stack-single:absent:focus-export. stack-single schedules nothing. Unlike the other four this one is opt-in everywhere, so its absence here matters least.

min_severity.what: The HERALDYX_MIN_SEVERITY default: the floor below which the notifier stays quiet.

min_severity:stack-up:medium.why: stack-up is the local developer sandbox on one machine with one operator, where a medium-severity signal is worth reading and there is no mailbox to flood. The two real deployments sit at high. stack-k8s's manifest carries the same reasoning in a comment beside its own value. Read as a decision rather than a gap, but read by me from the code, not stated by anyone: if it is wrong, it is wrong here first.

ports.what: The fixed local port each component listens on. Two deployments putting the same component on different ports is what makes a runbook wrong.

ports:stack-k8s:unagreed:genaryx-console.why: Not a component port: `genaryx-console-lb` is a LoadBalancer Service in front of the console, so 443 is an ingress port and the console itself is still on the agreed 7420 in the same repo. It is deliberately EXCLUDED from stack-k8s's default kustomization because a cloud load balancer is metered, so a default install never creates it. stack-single reaches the same place with caddy. Recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'Services of this type do not count' is a decision and decisions belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

services.what: Which components each deployment brings up.

services:stack-up:absent:console.why: stack-up serves a static dashboard out of python3 -m http.server instead of running the genaryx console. Deliberate: the console is a built web application and stack-up's whole argument is that it needs nothing but the binaries it installs into ~/.taipan/bin.

services:stack-up:extra:dashboard.why: The other half of services:stack-up:absent:console. The static dashboard on port 3000 exists only in stack-up.

services:stack-up:absent:policy-db.why: wardryx keeps its store on local disk under stack-up rather than in postgres. Deliberate: a sandbox that needs a database server is not a sandbox.

services:stack-single:extra:wg.why: stack-single is the one deployment meant to be reached from outside the box, so it ships a WireGuard endpoint. stack-k8s does the same job in a separate tunnel overlay outside manifests/, and stack-up is loopback-only by invariant.

services:stack-single:extra:caddy.why: TLS termination in front of the console, for the same reason as wg. In stack-k8s the equivalent is the LoadBalancer manifest, which is excluded from the default apply because it is metered.

services:stack-single:extra:init-volumes.why: A one-shot busybox container that creates the shared volume layout, not a running component. Kubernetes gets the same effect from PersistentVolumeClaims in 00-base.yaml and stack-up from mkdir in up.sh.

services:stack-up:extra:vouchryx.why: A DECISION, and his: the estate is one product installed by function («з можливістю встановлення за окремими функціоналами»), and `delegate` is one of those functions rather than part of the base stack. stack-up gained it first because it is the sandbox; stack-single and stack-k8s are step 3 of agent-market-research-2026-08/PLAN.md section 8 and will follow. Recorded as `extra` rather than by adding vouchryx to `agreed` on purpose: `agreed` is what every deployment brings up, and an opt-in profile is not that. Measured 2026-08-27 on a real ./up.sh --with-delegation: the gateway reports `delegation door: ON` and refuses a revoked token with HTTP 401, while the same launcher without the flag returns 200 to that same revoked token because the door never examines it. NOTE for whoever adds the other two: this file's model has no notion of a PROFILE, only of agreed/extra/absent, so a second and third deployment installing vouchryx will read here as two more `extra` entries rather than as one decision. That is a limit of C5 worth fixing when it bites, not a reason to write the wrong thing now.

coverage.what: Both directions of the same question. Forwards: a component a repository's `runs` claims that no deployment installs. Backwards: a component a deployment installs that no repository claims. Subjects are DISCOVERED from estate.json's `runs` field and from what the deployments were read to install, never listed here. The second direction exists because `runs: []` is otherwise a way to leave this family with nothing to say: a repository that declares itself inert disappears from the check meant to find components nobody installs.

coverage:policy-db:claimed-by-no-reposit.why: A DECISION and not a gap: postgres, upstream. stack-single and stack-k8s run wardryx's store as a database server; no repository in this estate builds or owns it, so no `runs` can claim it. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:dashboard:claimed-by-no-reposit.why: A DECISION and not a gap: a static page stack-up serves with `python3 -m http.server`, and the other half of `services:stack-up:absent:console`. It is files in stack-up's own tree rather than a component any repository contributes. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:wg:claimed-by-no-repository.why: A DECISION and not a gap: WireGuard, upstream. stack-single is the one deployment meant to be reached from outside the box; see `services:stack-single:extra:wg`. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:caddy:claimed-by-no-repository.why: A DECISION and not a gap: Caddy, upstream. TLS termination in front of the console; see `services:stack-single:extra:caddy`. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:init-volumes:claimed-by-no-repo.why: A DECISION and not a gap: a one-shot busybox container that creates stack-single's shared volume layout. Not a running component and not anybody's product; see `services:stack-single:extra:init-volumes`. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.
